title: Given a string containing just the characters `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[` and `]`, determine if the input string is valid — brackets must be closed in the correct order by a matching pair.
shortTitle: Valid Parentheses — stack matching bracket pairs

s1_definition.profdef: Valid Parentheses is a classic stack problem where you verify that every opening bracket has a correctly ordered matching closing bracket. You push each opening bracket onto a stack, and when you meet a closing bracket you pop the top and check it is the matching opener. The string is valid only if every closing bracket matches and the stack is empty at the end.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh at National Bank of India opening nested approval requests. He opens a loan request, then inside it opens a document-verification request, then inside that a signature request. Each request he opens he writes on a sticky note and places on top of a pile. When a request closes, the one that closes must be the one on top of the pile — the most recently opened. If a signature request tries to close while a document request is still on top, the paperwork is out of order and the whole batch is rejected.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push every opener, and on every closer pop the top and check it matches — valid only if the stack ends empty.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Valid Parentheses is a classic stack problem where you verify that every opening bracket has a correctly ordered matching closing bracket. You push each opening bracket onto a stack, and when you meet a closing bracket you pop the top and check it is the matching opener. The string is valid only if every closing bracket matches and the stack is empty at the end.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh at National Bank of India opening nested approval requests. He opens a loan request, then inside it opens a document-verification request, then inside that a signature request. Each request he opens he writes on a sticky note and places on top of a pile. When a request closes, the one that closes must be the one on top of the pile — the most recently opened. If a signature request tries to close while a document request is still on top, the paperwork is out of order and the whole batch is rejected.

**One line to remember:** Push every opener, and on every closer pop the top and check it matches — valid only if the stack ends empty.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is Last-In-First-Out ordering, which is exactly what a `Deque` used as a stack gives you. You iterate through each character. When the character is an opening bracket, you push it. When it is a closing bracket, you must check two things: the stack is not empty, and the element you pop is the matching opener.

The cleanest way to match pairs is a small `Map` that maps each closing bracket to its expected opening bracket. For example, `pairs.put(')', '(')`. When you see a closing bracket `c`, you peek or pop and compare against `pairs.get(c)`. For example: `if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.pop() != pairs.get(c)) return false;`.

An empty-stack check before popping is essential. If the string starts with a closing bracket like `")("`, the stack is empty when you reach `)`, so you return false immediately. For example: `if (stack.isEmpty()) return false;` guards against this.

The final check matters just as much as the loop. A string like `"((("` never fails inside the loop because there are no closing brackets, but it leaves three items on the stack. So you must return `stack.isEmpty()` at the end. For example: `return stack.isEmpty();` captures both the balanced and the unbalanced-open cases.

The time complexity is linear in the length of the string because each character is pushed and popped at most once. The space complexity is also linear in the worst case, such as a string of all opening brackets, where the stack grows to the full length. A senior nuance is to prefer `ArrayDeque` over the legacy `Stack` class, because `Stack` extends `Vector` and is synchronized, which adds needless locking overhead in single-threaded parsing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the back-office system receives financial expression strings that describe nested fee and tax calculations, such as `"{[(base+fee)*tax]}"`. Before the calculation engine runs, it must confirm the brackets are balanced, because an unbalanced expression means a corrupt or truncated message and must be rejected, not evaluated. This is exactly how Valid Parentheses works — we scan the expression and confirm every grouping is opened and closed in the right order.

Problem 2 — The system also processes nested approval workflows encoded as bracket strings, where each bracket type represents a different approval level. If a signature-level bracket closes while a document-level bracket is still open, the workflow is malformed. This is exactly the matching-pair requirement of the stack solution — the closer must match the most recently opened opener.

The mini-project builds a `BracketValidator` service with a `validate(String expression)` method that returns a boolean, a `BracketValidationService` that wraps it with logging for the banking audit trail, and a runnable demo class that validates several real expression strings. Each class is a normal top-level class, and the demo uses `java.util.logging.Logger` with a clean formatter.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the string `"{[(base+fee)*tax]}"`.

Step 1: The validator starts with an empty stack and reads `{`. It is an opener, so `{` is pushed. The stack is now `{`.

Step 2: It reads `[`, another opener, and pushes it. The stack is now `{ [` with `[` on top.

Step 3: It reads `(`, pushes it. The stack is `{ [ (` with `(` on top.

Step 4: It reads the letters `base`, the `+`, and `fee`. These are not brackets, so nothing changes on the stack.

Step 5: It reads `)`. This is a closer. The stack is not empty, so it pops the top, which is `(`, and compares it to the expected opener for `)`, which is also `(`. They match, so the scan continues. The stack is back to `{ [`.

Step 6: It reads `*` and `tax`, which are ignored.

Step 7: It reads `]`. It pops `[`, which matches the expected opener for `]`. The stack is now `{`.

Step 8: It reads `}`. It pops `{`, which matches. The stack is now empty.

Step 9: The scan is finished. The stack is empty, so the method returns true and the service logs the expression as accepted.

```text
2026-10-26T16:16:16Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Expression Bracket Validator
2026-10-26T16:16:16Z [INFO] Expression ACCEPTED (balanced): {[(base+fee)*tax]}
2026-10-26T16:16:16Z [WARNING] Expression REJECTED (unbalanced): {[(base+fee]*tax)}
2026-10-26T16:16:16Z [WARNING] Expression REJECTED (unbalanced): (((
2026-10-26T16:16:16Z [WARNING] Expression REJECTED (unbalanced): )(
2026-10-26T16:16:16Z [INFO] Expression ACCEPTED (balanced): []{}()
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: "{[(base+fee)*tax]}"
    │
    ▼
  BracketValidator.validate()
    │ read '{' → push        stack: [ { ]
    │ read '[' → push        stack: [ {, [ ]
    │ read '(' → push        stack: [ {, [, ( ]
    │ read 'base+fee' → skip  stack unchanged
    │ read ')' → pop '('   stack: [ {, [ ]
    │ read '*tax' → skip      stack unchanged
    │ read ']' → pop '['   stack: [ { ]
    │ read '}' → pop '{'   stack: [ ]
    ▼
  stack.isEmpty() == true → VALID
    │
    ▼
  BracketValidationService → log.info("ACCEPTED")
    │
    ▼
  Output: true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Parentheses is the textbook example of when a stack is the right data structure, because the rule governing brackets is Last-In-First-Out: the bracket that closes must always be the one most recently opened. My approach is to scan the string once, push every opening bracket onto a stack, and on every closing bracket pop the top and confirm it is the matching opener. I keep a small map from each closing bracket to its expected opening bracket so the match check is a constant-time lookup rather than a chain of conditionals.

There are two failure cases I handle explicitly. The first is a closing bracket arriving when the stack is empty, which happens when a string starts with a closer, so I check for an empty stack before popping. The second is the string ending with brackets still open, which never trips an error inside the loop, so I return whether the stack is empty at the very end. Both checks together are what make the solution correct, and candidates who forget the final empty check pass strings like three open parentheses incorrectly.

The algorithm runs in linear time because each character is handled once, and it uses linear space in the worst case of an all-opening string. I always reach for ArrayDeque rather than the old Stack class, because Stack extends Vector and is synchronized, which adds pointless locking in a single-threaded parser.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to validate nested fee and tax expression strings before the calculation engine runs. An unbalanced expression signals a corrupt or truncated message, so rejecting it early and writing it to the audit log protects the engine from evaluating garbage and gives the operations team a clean trail of malformed inputs to investigate.
